newsitem.title: USA: Nabisco brings cracker back by popular demand.
newsitem.headline: Nabisco brings cracker back by popular demand.

text.p: Food giant Nabisco Holdings Corp. crumbled before the wave of complaints from angry New Englanders and said Tuesday it would once again start baking and shipping the region's favourite chowder cracker.

"We thought we were discontinuing a cracker. It was clear we would be interrupting history for too many people," Nabisco executive Mark Hosbein said when announcing the re-introduction of the company's Crown Pilot Crackers.

Crown Pilots, which were often referred to as hardtack or ship biscuits by 18th century sailors, were introduced in 1792 at a Newburyport, Mass., bakery, that became part of Nabisco -- the National Biscuit Co. - in 1898.
The cracker may not be flavorful, but it's potential demise brought about a storm of emotion.

"It's bland. It's tastes really good slathered with butter and dunked in chowder," said Richard Ryder, 57, of Eastham, Mass. on Cape Cod. Ryder complained to the New Jersey-based baking company on Christmas and was one of about 25 Crown Pilot fans invited to Boston for a shipboard press conference annoucing the product's return.

Nabisco halted production of the brand last fall, but a series of articles by Donna Damon, 46, in her local newspaper on Chebeague Island in Maine started an avalanche of more than 3,500 phone calls, letters and e-mail to the company demanding the crackers be reintroduced. Sales of the cracker amount to about $500,000 a year.
She credited her fellow islanders with showing "that even companies can be responsive even if they are worth almost $8 billion."
Damon likened the crackers "to apple pie and mother" for New Englanders, saying, "You look at the box and can remember the first time you had them."

The daughter of a fisherman and the brother of a lobsterman, Damon, who brought her 10-year-old son Tom to the press conference, said she was concerned that "New England would become homogenized" if the cracker's production was halted. "If we really mean to honour diversity in this country, this cracker is a part of it."
Nabisco's Hosbein said that beginning next week New Englanders could begin seeing their beloved chowder cracker again on store shelves.
